newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: EMU treaty offers some leeway - Germany's Rexrodt.
newsitem.headline: EMU treaty offers some leeway - Germany's Rexrodt.

text.p: German Economy Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Saturday the Maastricht treaty on Europe's single currency offered some leeway for countries attempting to meet the three percent budget deficit criterium.
"There is leeway but not much leeway," Rexrodt told reporters after meeting his Austrian and Swiss counterparts, Johann Farnleitner and Jean-Pascal Delamuraz, in this Alpine city.

The 1992 Maastricht treaty requires countries wanting to join Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) to meet a set of strict set of economic criteria in 1997, including keeping budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product and public debt to 60 percent.

Rexrodt said Germany was eager to do all it could to meet the deficit target this year in order to qualify for early EMU membership. "The German government is eager to come as close as possible to meeting the three percent," he said.
The minister added he was convinced both Germany and France would be among the founding members of the single currency.
"I am convinced that in any case Germany and France have to be in," he said. "I am also convinced that Austria will be part (of the first group)."

Referring to next year's decision about which countries will qualify for early EMU membership, the minister said: "The treaty is talking about convergence and sustainability. (Countries) will be measured according to the sustainability of their results."
Rexrodt added the German government backed the inclusion of an Employment Chapter in the Maastricht II treaty to be discussed at a European Union summit in Amsterdam next week.

"The German side wants the stability pact to be agreed upon as it has been discussed over the past months," Rexrodt said, adding that Germany remained opposed to a previous French proposal for an "economic government" which Bonn fears could meddle with monetary policy decisions.
